from.target: Perimeter is the fence; area is the floor
essentialFacts: Perimeter is the distance around the outside: add up every side.
Area is the space covered inside: multiply length by width.
Fence, frame, trim, and border mean perimeter; carpet, paint, sod, and tile mean area.
from.aiExample: PeRIMeter has RIM in it: the rim goes around. AREA sounds like 'a rug': a rug covers the floor.
from.mapping: The hidden word rim points to the edge, and the sound-alike rug points to covering, so each word carries its own picture of around versus inside.
from.scaffoldStarter: Perimeter has ____ in it, which goes ____. Area sounds like ____, which ____.
scaffoldSteps: Find a hidden word or sound in each term.
Match it to around or inside.
Sort three jobs from the anchor chart with your hooks.
coachPrompts: Using your hooks, which one do you need to buy baseboard trim?
from.studentPrompt: Make your own two word hooks.
from.reasoningPrompt: How do your hooks stop you from mixing the two up on a test?

essentialFacts: Picture covering the yard with 1-foot square tiles: 8 tiles in a row, 5 rows, 40 tiles.
Multiplication is fast repeated addition of those rows.
Area is measured in square feet because you are literally counting squares; perimeter is in plain feet because it is a length.
from.aiExample: See the floor as a sheet of graph paper laid over the yard. Every little square is one square foot. Counting the squares IS the area, and the word square is right there in the answer.
from.mapping: The graph paper makes the unit visible: the answer's name comes from the shape you are counting, so square units stop being a rule and become a picture.
from.scaffoldStarter: I picture the floor covered in ____. Each one is a ____. Counting them gives the ____.
scaffoldSteps: Draw a small rectangle on grid paper.
Count the squares, then multiply the sides; check they match.
Say why the answer is square units.
coachPrompts: What would you be counting for the perimeter, and why is that not squares?
from.studentPrompt: Make your own tile picture for a room you know.
from.reasoningPrompt: How does your picture explain the word square in square feet?

hookFact.text: Writing '40 feet' for an area is not a small slip; it describes a different quantity entirely.

from.target: Same fence, different floor: same perimeter, different area
essentialFacts: 24 feet of fence as a 6 by 6 square gives an area of 36 square feet.
The same 24 feet as a 2 by 10 rectangle gives only 20 square feet.
The more square-like the rectangle, the more area you get from the same perimeter.
from.aiExample: Two neighbors buy the same 24 feet of fence. One builds 6 by 6 and gets 36 squares of grass. The other builds 2 by 10, a skinny dog run, and gets 20. Same fence, different floor. The square neighbor's dog is happier.
from.mapping: Two characters with the same fence make the surprise concrete: the chain goes fence, shape, area, and the ending shows which shape wins.
from.scaffoldStarter: Two neighbors both have ____ feet of fence. One builds ____ by ____ and gets ____. The other builds ____ by ____ and gets ____.
scaffoldSteps: Pick a fence length that makes two easy rectangles.
Say which shape wins and why.
coachPrompts: Can you make a third neighbor with an even smaller yard from the same fence?
from.reasoningPrompt: How does your story show that perimeter does not decide area?

hookFact.text: For rectangles, a square wins every time. If you allow any shape at all, a circle beats even the square.

from.context: The school garden club has been given 24 feet of fencing and a patch of ground along a wall. They want as much growing space as they can get. The garden also has to fit against the wall and leave a path for a wheelbarrow.
from.audience: The garden club and the teacher who will approve the build
from.drivingQuestion: Which rectangle made from exactly 24 feet of fence gives the most area? And does that shape still work for what the club needs?
from.seedDirection: First list every whole-number rectangle with a perimeter of 24. There are only a few. Work out each area before you argue.
lockedLessonFacts: Perimeter is the distance around the outside: add all four sides.
Area is the space covered inside: length times width, in square units.
Two rectangles can have the same perimeter and different areas; 6 by 6 gives 36 square feet and 2 by 10 gives 20 from the same 24 feet.
The more square-like the rectangle, the more area from the same perimeter.
openQuestions: Does the wall count as one side, so the fence only has to cover three sides?
How wide does the wheelbarrow path need to be?
Is the biggest area always the best garden? Or does shape matter for reaching the plants?
stakeholders: Students who will weed and water from the path
criteria: A table of every whole-number rectangle with perimeter 24 and its area
The chosen design is drawn with labeled sides, and both measurements use the right units
The explanation says why you picked that shape, and names any tradeoff
Uses at least three glossary words correctly
constraints: Exactly 24 feet of fence, whole-number sides
Must leave a path at least 3 feet wide beside the garden
from.deliverable: A labeled drawing of the garden with its perimeter and area. The table of all the options. And a short note to the club that explains your choice.
